Business.title: College students rally in support of Starbucks baristas urging boycott over contract negotiations
Business.text:
Starbucks baristas, students, elected officials and allies are planning rallies at over 40 college campuses across the US on Thursday to support the Starbucks Workers United boycott campaign as the union nears five years of deadlock with the company over contract negotiations.

Starbucks Workers United is seeking better pay and stronger staffing levels, including a $17 an hour minimum wage for baristas and a minimum staffing of three workers per store. It has called on the public to boycott Starbucks until its first contract is reached.

More than 700 Starbucks stores have voted to unionize, representing more than 12,000 baristas. It typically takes over 450 days for a new labor union to negotiate and reach its first contract, but it has been nearly five years since the first Starbucks store in Buffalo, New York, voted to unionize in December 2021.

Starbucks Workers United began to focus on college campuses in 2023, calling on campuses to cancel their contracts with Starbucks in protest against the company’s response to union-organizing efforts. In response, Cornell University and Pomona College did not renew their contracts with the company, while UCLA stopped offering Starbucks products in their cafes.

Rallies and events will take place at private and public universities across the country, including the University of Pennsylvania, Northwestern and the University of Washington.

The union push come ahead of the company’s busy holiday season, including Starbucks’ Red Cup Day on 17 November, when customers receive a reusable holiday cup.

“Starbucks has been fueling the working class for decades, but they’re failing the workers that fuel their profits,” said Andrew Trinklein, a barista who is participating in an event at the University of Texas at Austin. “We’re really trying to push and get support from college campus students… in joining the boycott.”

His store recently unionized, and he expressed shock at how the company hired pricey union avoidance consultants in attempts to deter workers from unionizing. Starbucks has reportedly spent tens of millions of dollars related to union avoidance, though it has not disclosed the full costs relating to its union-organizing efforts.

Trinklein emphasized that employees are currently employed at-will, meaning they have no just-cause job security protections.

“Right now it’s just a toss-up whether we have a job tomorrow or not. Say they don’t like something that we’re doing – say we don’t write on a cup. We could be fired for it tomorrow,” Trinklein said, referring to the company’s policy requiring employees to write friendly messages on cups for customers. “But with this contract, that won’t be possible. We’ll have protections from stuff like that.”

Efforts to pressure Starbucks to negotiate were temporarily paused when the union and Starbucks reached an agreement on a path forward in February 2024. But negotiations broke down shortly after Brian Niccol took over as Starbucks CEO.

Niccol previously served as CEO of Chipotle from 2018 to 2024, and under his tenure, the company agreed to pay $240,000 to former workers as part of a settlement over a store closing in Maine after it unionized, which the National Labor Relations Board said was illegal. Chipotle has denied wrongdoing.

In recent years, Starbucks has been found to have violated federal labor law by the NLRB in several cases regarding its responses to union-organizing efforts. Starbucks has challenged these rulings.

In a statement, a Starbucks spokesperson said: “Workers United represents approximately 5% of our US partners, and we believe actions like these divert attention from the work at the bargaining table.”

“Our partners and coffeehouses are focused on bringing the joy of the holidays to life for our customers. Based on our experience with prior similar actions, we don’t expect any meaningful disruption and look forward to serving our customers through the holidays,” a spokesperson for Starbucks wrote in an email.

The spokesperson noted that “according to independent research, Starbucks offers the best overall pay and benefits in the industry, worth on average more than $30 per hour and including comprehensive healthcare, 100% upfront tuition coverage, company stock and up to 18 weeks of paid parental leave for partners working as little as 20 hours a week, which is why our turnover is among the industry’s lowest, and nearly 3 million people applied to wear the green apron last year”.

Business.title: Home sales hit 16-year low in October amid soaring mortgage rates
Business.text:
US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Mortgage rates had been steadily declining in 2024 and 2025, with the 30-year rate falling below 6% for the first time in February 2026. But increasing inflation and higher interest rates amid the Iran war have pushed rates back up to a nearly three-year high.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which is the most commonly used rate in home loans, is now hovering at about 7.18%, not far from its 2023 high of 7.79%. During the pandemic, average mortgage rates were just above 3%.

“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Lawrence Yun, chief economist at the NAR. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Pending home sales, or the number of contracts that have been signed before closing, reached its lowest levels in the NAR’s history in September, the same month that the 30-year mortgage rate topped 7% for the first time in nearly two years.

Mortgage rates have been directly affected by interest rate changes by the US Federal Reserve, which in September hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023. Rates currently sit at a range of 3.75% to 4%.

The central bank is poised to raise rates again next month to combat heightened inflation, which went up more than expected in October.

Affordability and cost-of-living concerns played an outsized role in the midterm elections that gave Democrats control of Congress next year. According to the latest census data, growth in median rent across the US outpaced inflation. The home-ownership rate in the US has stagnated since 2021, according to the same data.

Business.title: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
Business.text:
Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.

Early odds suggest a Democrat may win the presidential election in two years, a fitting coda to last week’s broad rejection of the Maga brand of politics. It’s not beyond hope to expect a Democratic trifecta that will spend less time on settling grievances and more on fixing a threadbare social safety net that allows for the deepest poverty in the affluent world.

And yet, the post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money. The federal deficit is now running at about 6.2% of GDP. The federal debt hit $40tn, more than 120% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Paying interest on that debt costs some 3.2% of GDP. That’s about $1tn, more than is spent on national defense. The Congressional Budget Office projects that debt and interest payments will continue to grow faster than the economy over the coming decades. In October alone, the first month of the 2027 fiscal year, the fiscal deficit ballooned to $409bn.

The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that restoring the subsidies to health insurance plans under Obamacare from 2030 to 2039 would cost $460bn. Undoing the budget cuts to the Snap food stamp program and Medicaid that Trump used to partly fund the tax cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) would cost $2.2tn over that decade. “Reversing the harms is going to be very expensive,” said CBPP’s senior director for Federal budget policy, Brendan Duke.

And that’s the easy part. The trust fund that pays for social security benefits is scheduled to run out of money in less than six years, when the new crop of Democratic senators are still in their first term. By law, that would lead to an automatic 22% cut in benefits. Fixing that will require more money. Artificial intelligence may further complicate the picture, burdening the safety net with potentially millions of workers displaced by the new technological revolution.

Historian Bruce Bartlett, who back in the day advised Ronald Reagan on budget policy, argues that this state of affairs is the outcome of a Republican strategy honed over the years since Gipper’s day: cut taxes to strangle the budget and tie the hands of whatever Democratic administration comes next.

Trump’s OBBBA will add somewhere between $4.1tn and $5.5tn to the federal debt over 10 years, depending on whether temporary tax cuts in the bill are made permanent by a future Congress, something that has usually happened in the past. This, Bartlett once told me, will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”.

The new taxes that would be needed just to fill the holes Trump and his Republican enablers bored into the budget, let alone patch up the safety net they gleefully eviscerated, seem beyond anything achieved in recent memory.

Consider this: The last time that a government with any Republican in power delivered a tax increase was in the 1990s, when George HW Bush was president and Congress was blue. Bush paid for his sin, though, losing reelection to Democrat Bill Clinton. And that was the end of that.

Democrats have raised money when they held the presidency and Congress. But the trend suggests the opportunities are fading. Bill Clinton’s 1993 tax increases are estimated to yield the equivalent of $3.3tn over the 2030-2039 decade, adjusting for inflation. But the feat, which helped produce the nation’s first budget surplus since the 1960s, was ultimately spent on a tax cut by Clinton’s successor, George W. Bush.

The next shot at raising taxes was more modest. Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act raised the equivalent of $1.1tn over 2030-2039, in inflation-adjusted dollars. But Obama also made permanent some of George W Bush’s tax cuts. Joe Biden tried to go bigger: his original Build Back Better Act, passed in the House, would have raised the equivalent of $2.3tn over that window. But the Senate nixed that, authorizing only about $700bn in the Inflation Reduction Act.

How much more tax revenue does the US need? It depends on what Democrats want to achieve. Total tax revenue in the US amounts to less than 26% of its gross domestic product. That is 9 percentage points less than Britain’s total tax take, as a share of its economy, 9.5 points less than Canada’s, 12.5 points less than Germany’s and 16 percentage points less than Sweden’s.

Perhaps matching other rich countries is an impossibly high bar. Still, Democrats must prove that they understand the new America they hope to build comes with a price tag they are willing to fight for.

Some tax cuts in Trump’s OBBBA are set to expire in the next couple of years: exemptions on income from tips and overtime, a new deduction for seniors and an increase in the deduction for state and local taxes. The CBPP observed that these cuts offer next to nothing to Americans on the bottom rungs of the income distribution. Extending them would cost about $1.2tn over the 10-year window.

Will Democrats have the guts to end them? That will be the test of whether America is ready for a new social contract or not.

Business.title: Federal judge allows Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against BBC to proceed
Business.text:
Federal judge Jeffrey T Kuntz ruled on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the BBC can proceed, denying in part the British broadcaster’s motion to dismiss the case. The president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit stems from the BBC’s splicing together of disparate comments he made before the 6 January US Capitol insurrection, as rendered in a Panorama documentary called Trump: A Second Chance.

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” the Trump-appointed Florida district court judge wrote. “It would be difficult for the Court to accept a different framing without completely negating the significance and fragility of political elections.”

The judge noted the significance of the documentary’s editing decision, which spliced together comments made by Trump that were nearly 55 minutes apart, something the BBC has apologized for.

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” he wrote. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The judge continued: “Editing is often required. However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement. This was not trimming around the edges but creating something different than what was stated in the speech.”

The judge noted past errors in the broadcaster’s coverage and wrote that “such examples can be said to be probative of BBC’s state of mind as it pertains to recklessness in light of BBC’s non-action toward false statements about Trump. Thus, Trump paints a picture that demonstrates the BBC has a record of allowing the publication of false statements in their portrayal of Trump.”

The judge also wrote that “Trump’s allegations regarding BBC’s departure from journalistic standards are more than enough to plausibly alleged more than mere negligence”.

The BBC released a statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Trump heralded the ruling on Truth Social, calling it a “huge victory”. “We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” Trump said.

While the judge determined that Trump had “sufficiently pleaded” that the BBC acted with actual malice, the legal standard for a public figure to win a defamation case, he will have to actually prove they did so at trial.

The judge also dismissed Trump’s claim that the BBC violated Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

And the judge determined that the president will have to prove that he suffered “actual damages” from the airing of the document, which was not broadcast in Florida.

Business.title: US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped
Business.text:
US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.

But the newest data shows that prices are still increasing at a moderate pace. Economists estimate that, if interpolating the data for October 2025, the topline inflation figure for October 2026 would have been 3.9%, according to Oxford Economics. That would have been the highest its been since May 2026, when inflation reached 4.2%, a three-year high.

Higher energy costs driven by the Iran war have been the main factor behind increased inflation. Energy prices continued to rise slightly in October, rising 0.7% after going up 5.2% in September. In September, the overall monthly change in CPI from August was 0.6%.

The new data comes after a midterm election that will give Democrats control of Congress, in what was largely seen as a rebuke of Republicans over high prices. In their postmortem of the midterms, Republicans, including JD Vance, have specifically pointed to frustration over increased gas prices as a reason why the party fared so poorly in the election.

Gas prices cooled slightly in October, dropping from an average of $4.41 a gallon at the beginning of the month to $4.22 a gallon, prices are still more than $1 a gallon higher than a year ago, according to AAA. On Monday, the average price for a gallon at the pump fell below $4 for the first time since July.

The cost of diesel, which is used to power trucks, farming equipment, buses and trains, is nearly $2.50 a gallon higher compared with prices last year but has also been going down since October. Gas prices have continued to drop.

In September, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and are expected to hike rates again at their next meeting in December. Higher interest rates slow the economy by making borrowing money more expensive, and can slow inflation. The Fed’s target inflation rate is 2%, which it considers a stable pace for price increases.

Growth in the labor market surpassed economists’ expectations in October, giving more room for the Fed to hike rates. The unemployment rate has been relatively steady, hovering just above 4%.

Because today’s inflation is so closely tied to energy prices, it’s unclear how much and how quickly a rate hike could ease prices. But the Fed’s chair, Kevin Warsh, said the central bank is dedicated to making sure price increases ease up.

“Our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored,” Warsh said on 28 October.

Consumer sentiment increased slightly at the end of October as gas prices eased, according to the University of Michigan’s Survey of Consumers. At the same time, the US stock market was experiencing a dip as investors voiced skepticism over the influx of AI spending.

“While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of ​a relatively ​turbulent period ⁠in stock markets,” said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers, in a statement. “Moreover, ​consumers’ comments revealed growing anxiety over ​a ⁠possible AI bubble.”

Sports.title: Spain 2-3 England: Three Lions produce best win under Thomas Tuchel
Sports.text:
Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.

In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.

Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."

To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.

It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final.

If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.

The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?

Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?

The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.

Not a backward step was taken.

This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.

But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.

Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?

"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.

"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."

Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.

Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.

What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.

England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.

It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.

England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.

From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.

When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.

In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.

Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".

There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.

Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.

If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.

Yes. And yes.

Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.

The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.

But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.

And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.

"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.

"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.

"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."

England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.

The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.

After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.

England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.

"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.

"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."

Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.

"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."

Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was...

Sports.title: Spain 2-3 England: How did Thomas Tuchel's side win and what was learned from Argentina defeat?
Sports.text:
England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.

But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.

So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.

England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.

Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.

But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.

"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."

Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.

In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.

Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.

But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.

However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.

The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.

And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.

However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.

"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.

"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.

"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."

England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.

In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.

Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.

In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.

In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.

"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We defended in a 4-4-1," he continued.

"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."

England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.

But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.

So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?

After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.

"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.

"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."

Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.

"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.

Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.

He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.

Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

Sports.title: DP World Tour Championship: Rory McIlroy claims Race To Dubai as Tyrell Hatton wins tournament
Sports.text:
DP World Tour Championship final leaderboard

-15 Hatton (Eng); -10 McIlroy (NI); -8 Chacarra (Spa), Lindell (Fin); -7 Olesen (Den), Reitan (Nor), Laporta (Ita), Lindberg (Swe), Perez (Fra)

Selected others: -4 Wallace (Eng); -3 Rahm (Spa), Schaper (SA); Level Fleetwwod (Eng), Reed (US), Fox (NZ); +1 Rai (Eng)

Rory McIlroy wiped away tears as he dedicated his eighth Race to Dubai victory to his ill father, Gerry.

Moments after matching Colin Montgomerie's record of season-long European tour titles on Sunday, the Northern Irishman was asked about the health of his father.

An emotional McIlroy revealed Gerry has been in hospital for two months after "a huge operation" - a double lung transplant - at the end of September.

"He's recovering well, thankfully," McIlroy told the DP World Tour.

"But before I left to come here to the Middle East, I went up to Cleveland to see him. He said to me: 'Go win The Race to Dubai'.

"This one's for him."

It came after a thrilling climax at the traditional season-ending DP World Tour Championship with Tyrrell Hatton securing a commanding victory, while McIlroy pipped Spaniard Eugenio Chacarra to the overall crown.

Hatton's closing six-under-par 66 helped him romp to a five-shot victory on 15 under par but most eyes were on the thrilling battle that went down to the final hole.

It is the fifth successive year that McIlroy has won the award and it has drawn him level with Montgomerie, the Scot who set a mark 21 years ago that few thought would ever be matched.

"Yeah, double digits," smiled McIlroy when asked what would be his final target of Race to Dubai victories.

"I'd love to surpass Monty next year and we'll go from there."

McIlroy's confidence in going along with a target shouted out by the fans surrounding the 18th green at the Earth Course in Dubai on Sunday was refreshing to hear.

But he appears to be playing and talking with a little more freedom in recent years - the sort of freedom that comes as a result of finally completing the career Grand Slam and winning successive Masters titles - and leads to declarations of winning 10, or more.

"Winning eight Order of Merits (Race to Dubai titles) was never in my list of goals growing up," said McIlroy, who closed with a bogey-free 67 to finish on 10 under and must surely now be considered Europe's greatest golfer.

"I remember Monty being a stalwart of the European tour and playing with him at the London Club in 2008, so to pull up alongside him and win eight of these means the world to me."

After Jon Rahm's victory in Abu Dhabi last week, fellow former LIV Golf member Hatton showed his class with a five-shot success at the Earth Course at Jumeirah Golf Estates.

Hatton showed his combustible side earlier in the week but, despite later admitting to being "weirdly nervous" he appeared serene on Sunday.

In the final group and knowing he couldn't win the overall Race to Dubai title, he was detached enough to block out the scramble as he strolled to his ninth DP World Tour victory - even asking an on-course reporter who was going to win as he walked from the 17th green to 18th tee.

It was that head-to-head battle between Chacarra and McIlroy that dominated the tournament, a battle that, after a long hard season, came right down to the wire.

Both players knew victory would win them the title. There were permutations galore for finishing second, third, or below that.

Chacarra and McIlroy went toe-to-toe in and the overall lead in the rankings chopped and changed down an absorbing back nine as neither man backed down.

At one juncture just one-tenth of a point separated the pair.

But a late surge from Northern Ireland's McIlroy allowed him to finish runner-up behind England's Hatton in the tournament and collect enough points to edge out the gutsy Spaniard.

Chacarra, who earned around $15-20m during three years as a LIV player, is in just his second season on the DP World Tour. He is the only three-time winner of this year's campaign and was desperate to add his name to compatriots Rahm and Seve Ballesteros as the third Spanish order of merit winner.

After four early birdies he looked in fine shape. The pressure began to tell as he posted three bogeys in four holes around the turn. But he responded brilliantly with two more birdies to push McIlroy all the way.

Chacarra, the 26-year-old world number 39, finished in a tie for third to end up second in the overall standings and earn a PGA Tour card for next season.

After this latest addition to McIlroy's glowing CV it's hard to make a case against him being Europe's greatest ever golfer – and as he continues to find new targets to stay motivated one of them is very much to unequivocally nail down that title.

Motivation was a problem in the immediate aftermath of finally ending his long wait to win the Masters in 2025 as he became just the sixth man to win the career Grand Slam.

But a year later he had re-found it as he became just the fourth back-to-back Green Jacket winner with his brilliant defence at Augusta National back in April.

That put him on six major titles, level with England's Sir Nick Faldo and just one behind the great Harry Vardon, whose name adorns the trophy McIlroy has just hoisted for the eighth time.

Still only 37, McIlroy still has plenty of time to overhaul Montgomerie and hold the outright record for the most European number one titles – despite playing on two tours throughout the majority of his career.

Targets have changed – McIlroy is not chasing the world number one spot or winning any old trophy. He's voiced his desire to focus on majors, play more in Europe and around the globe and keep stacking up these order of merit titles.

An Olympic title is perhaps the only honour missing from his trophy cabinet, and he will have the chance to change that in 2028 on a familiar Riviera Country Club Course, which is a regular stop-off on the PGA Tour and where he finished second a this year's Genesis Invitational.

He will be attempting to become the first man to win three Masters in a row next April, before the US Open at Pebble Beach and Open Championship at St Andrews offer great chances at venues McIlroy knows he can thrive on.

McIlroy has won six Ryder Cups as a stalwart for Europe and is just seven points behind all-time leader Sergio Garcia.

But even if the Northern Irishman quit the game right now he's already built a more than compelling argument that he's the greatest player the continent has ever seen.

Sports.title: Gregor Townsend hails Scotland's defence in Australia 'arm wrestle'
Sports.text:
Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend hailed his team's defensive efforts after they edged past Australia in a Nations Championship "arm wrestle" at Murrayfield.

Off the back of being dismantled by New Zealand last weekend, in which they failed to score a second half point, the spotlight fell on Scotland's leaky defence.

But on a chilly and damp Edinburgh day where physicality was king, they delivered a much-needed win and showed they are capable of winning ugly.

Even so, Townsend's side didn't make it easy.

Max Jorgensen's late converted try gave the Wallabies hope, and with the clock in the red, the visitors broke from their own half.

Murrayfield held its breath, but Darcy Graham hauled Australia full-back Tom Wright into touch with a superb tackle.

"When we saw the rain half an hour before kick-off, you still hope you'll be able to move the ball," Townsend said.

"You could tell defences were coming off the line a bit quicker, knowing they could pressure the ball carrier.

"Both teams had to adjust and I thought we did that well. Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years. Set after set we were putting them under pressure.

"We were on that edge of physicality but disciplined, hitting hard in the tackle, putting pressure on, listening to the referee, getting back onside. That makes it hard for the opposition to get into our 22m, which was a learning from last week.

"It was just constant effort. Today, we showed we can play another game, too."

Leading 12-5 at half-time, there was one eye on whether Scotland could clinch a bonus-point victory that would have both boosted their points difference and helped their chances of climbing the northern hemisphere table with Japan to come on Saturday.

However, it soon became apparent that would not be forthcoming in a match that will not live long in the memory.

"It was about winning at all costs today," former Scotland prop Peter Wright said.

"We hoped we might get something quite end-to-end, 50 points to 48, loads of tries, but to come out on the right end of a war of attrition like that, it's a good feeling.

"When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style at any sport. We just want to get victories under our belt.

"It was a bad game last week so getting some momentum going into the Japan game next week was really important.

"I thought the pack was outstanding."

In the absence of Sione Tuipulotu, who was ruled out of playing against the country of his birth with a knee injury, Rory Darge captained Scotland and led from the front with a player-of-the-match display.

The Glasgow Warriors flanker was immense in contact and at the breakdown, and also had the presence of mind to tell Finn Russell to kick at goal instead of going to the corner in the closing stages.

The resulting three points put Scotland 10 points in front and proved to be the winning score.

Townsend praised the performance his stand-in skipper, while also pointing to a wider effort defensively.

"He's always important," he said.

"You know the opposition will get phases of attack and we'll have to defend. Rory with his tackling, with his effort and his post-tackle presence really helps us.

"There were a lot of other players that stood up physically. The shots that were going in, the effort going in was outstanding."

And Darge himself was heartened by how Scotland responded to the All Blacks loss.

"We were disappointed after last week's performance," he said.

"A lot of that disappointment was with the physical side of the game and we did that really well.

"It was a bit of an arm wrestle, the conditions played their part. We know they want to throw the ball around, we like to play an attacking style but today was a battle of the defences."

Sports.title: WTA Finals: Mirra Andreeva beats Elina Svitolina to win season-ending title at Indian Wells
Sports.text:
For Mirra Andreeva, the thought of her first WTA Finals singles campaign was so stressful that it gave her "a little breakdown" in a practice session before the tournament.

The 19-year-old may have been nervous on arrival at Indian Wells, but she leaves California as the champion, having been the standout player of the week.

The French Open winner produced a hard-fought 7-5 6-3 victory over Elina Svitolina in Sunday's final to become the youngest champion of the event in 22 years.

The Russian has now risen to second in the world rankings - and she will start the 2027 season just 293 points behind top-ranked Elena Rybakina.

Andreeva did not drop a set on her way to the title and lost only 26 games across her five matches.

She raised her arms in celebration after beating Svitolina before racing to celebrate with her team, which includes 1994 Wimbledon champion Conchita Martinez.

"I am super thankful to my team for pushing me to my limits, for forcing me to do stuff when I don't want to do anything," Andreeva said.

"Thanks for fighting with me, thanks for forcing me to do everything that I have to do and not asking any questions!"

As well as £2.55m in prize money, Andreeva also won a custom purple Mercedes - and joked she was happy to remain a "passenger princess" until she passed her test.

One of the most notable parts of Andreeva's performance has been her increased maturity.

In March, she swore at the Indian Wells crowd after suffering an early defeat in the venue's WTA Tour tournament, and she has struggled to control her emotions, external on court in the past.

However, she showed little sign of that during this tournament.

Against Svitolina, one of the grittiest players on the women's tour, she lost a break lead three times across the two sets. Each time, she reset admirably, upping her aggression on her backhand in particular to put pressure back on her opponent.

After losing serve in a mammoth nine-minute game in the second set, Andreeva marched back to her chair and then broke Svitolina from 40-0 down in the next game to stay in front.

While her serve was not at its best, Andreeva still saved nine of the 12 break points she faced and hit 19 winners to Svitolina's 10.

"This fighting mindset helped me to get more brave and aggressive in the important moments," Andreeva told Sky Sports.

"This is just a dream. I had a little breakdown in my practice just before Indian Wells because I was so stressed.

"I didn't want to lose a match in the group. It's amazing."

Andreeva had only won one of her six matches against top-10 players in 2026 coming into the tournament.

She has beaten three top-10 players en route to the title, including a demolition of four-time major champion Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday.

She also laughed off an incident before the tournament where private comments Jessica Pegula made to her coach about Andreeva - including calling her a "diva" - were live-streamed.

Just as she did when she won the French Open, Andreeva ended her speech by thanking herself - a twist on a quote she "stole" from rapper Snoop Dogg.

"I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work and for never quitting," she said.

"For not taking the days off, for working every day and committing to what I have to do - just thanks to myself."

Sports.title: Ronaldinho makes comeback for Ravenna
Sports.text:
Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.

The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.

He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.

The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.

He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.

At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.

Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.

A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.

The game was streamed in several countries around the world.

Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.

A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.

In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.

He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.

He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.

Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.

"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.

And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."

Sports.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Has tournament set a new benchmark for international rugby league?
Sports.text:
Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?

It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.

The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear,, external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.

But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.

For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.

Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.

England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.

And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.

"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.

"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.

"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."

That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.

The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.

That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.

For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.

While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams., external

Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.

With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.

Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.

That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.

Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.

France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.

Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.

"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.

"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.

"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.

"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."

A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits, external before a ball was kicked.

The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.

In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".

And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.

And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.

Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.

Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.

This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.

In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.

Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.

Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.

"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."

In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."

And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.

The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.

Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.

Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.

And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

Sports.title: Women's Super League: London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit
Sports.text:
After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.

Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.

Eder Maestre's side sit third in the table - the last qualification spot for next season's Women's Champions League - and are six points above Arsenal.

It is a strong position to be in just shy of the halfway stage having already faced big hitters Arsenal, Manchester City and Manchester United.

Current leaders Chelsea await in December but, for now, London City's progress is moving at a pace that looks set to challenge the usual suspects.

A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.

They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.

The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.

Maestre said after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents showed more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.

They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.

That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves.

"The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," said Maestre.

"The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game shows we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these big games.

"We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent.

"We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win."

That bravery showed as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.

London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.

Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.

But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off.

"We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre.

"We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those."

London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a big difference in the transfer market.

They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.

Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench.

Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.

She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.

Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games.

"Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," said Maestre.

"She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches.

"I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her."

Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.

The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.

She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week.

"I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre.

"She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?

"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her."

Sports.title: Formula 1: Lewis Hamilton says 'much still to do' to improve sport's diversity
Sports.text:
Lewis Hamilton says there is "much still to do" when it comes to increasing diversity in Formula 1.

The seven-time champion has used a report published on the five-year anniversary of establishing his Mission 44 charity, external to demand three key steps from the sport.

The campaign seeks to increase the representation of black people, women and people from lower socio-economic backgrounds in F1.

The report recognises that all parts of the industry have made steps to increase diversity.

But it said the sport did not have the data to show whether these efforts had "changed who enters, progresses and stays in motorsport".

Hamilton said: "When I walk through the paddock now, I see more women, more Black and Brown faces, more people who look like the fans in the grandstands than at any point since I started. That is heartening, and the people behind it deserve credit.

"And yet, there is much still to do. We have opened the door, but we have not yet learned to count how many people walk through it, or how many stay.

"The sport's first social impact report shows how much is happening. This report asks what it adds up to. This is a sport that measures performance to the thousandth of a second. We can measure this too."

The Mission 44 report makes three recommendations:

Measure who joins, who is promoted and who stays, and let the best practice be recognised.

Take investment in people out of the F1 cost cap and put money behind the pipeline collectively.

Publish the paid places being offered every year.

An F1 spokesperson said: "We are proud of the programmes and initiatives which help inspire the next generation of Formula 1 and how they continue to increase access and opportunity across our sport.

"Following recommendations from the Hamilton Commission, the sport signed its first ever diversity and inclusion charter in 2024, and in 2025 conducted its first ever sport-wide data gathering exercise to capture the global reach of our social impact programmes, external.

"This showed that in 2025 season alone, more than 500,000 young people engaged in education, STEM and inspiration programmes globally and over 1,000 structured skills and talent development opportunities across our sport.

"As F1 continues to grow on the global stage, so too does our ambition to deepen and evolve our social impact. We are committed, alongside the F1 teams, the FIA and broader members of our sport to continue build on this foundation and look forward to sharing the next phase of our work."

The Mission 44 report proposes that F1, governing body the FIA, the teams and the sport's main sponsors "invest at least £50m of new money over the next five years into supporting young people from underrepresented backgrounds into motorsport careers, and supporting them to stay".

It said it was not able to say whether activity related to diversity was succeeding in increasing numbers because there was "no collated data on the entire motorsports workforce, only on the 'activity and reach' of social impact programmes".

It added: "Figures are self-reported through a structured data request.

"However, we cannot see who is recruited as a result of the activity, who stays or who progresses in their career.

"The data does not record demographic details of who participated in the programmes, and teams define underrepresented groups differently, so even where numbers exist, they cannot be compared.

"The original question of the Hamilton Commission was how many Black people worked in motorsport. Five years on, the sport cannot say exactly how that number has changed."

The report recognised examples of improvement in diversity at teams who reported figures. Not all did.

Mercedes set itself a target in 2020 to improve representation of underrepresented groups in its workforce after data showed only 3% of were from minority ethnic backgrounds, and 12% were women.

After implementing training, recruitment and development processes for hiring, by 2025 Mercedes reported 20% of employees were women, 10% were from minority ethnic backgrounds, and 37% of new joiners in the first half of that year were from underrepresented groups.

McLaren publishes detailed workforce data every year and its 2025 sustainability report showed that 36% of staff identified with one or more underrepresented characteristics, against a 2030 target of 40%, and 44.8% of new starters in 2025 were from underrepresented groups.

Women make up 22% of McLaren F1's workforce and 10% of technical functions, with that latter number up from 7% the year before.

All the F1 teams, F1 itself and governing body the FIA have signed up to a diversity and inclusion charter, external.

F1 realised its first sport-wide social impact report last month and reported a series of steps to increase diversity and inclusion.

Sports.title: Grand Slam of Darts: Beau Greaves and Jonny Clayton knocked out at the group stage
Sports.text:
Beau Greaves was eliminated from the Grand Slam of Darts at the group stage despite ending her campaign with a win over Niels Zonneveld in Wolverhampton.

Greaves, 22, beat Dutchman Zonneveld 5-3 but it was not enough to keep her in the competition after Saturday's heavy defeat by Luke Littler.

The three-time women's world champion fought back impressively from 3-1 down, winning three consecutive legs to take the lead in the best-of-five match.

She missed two match darts in a tense final leg but 28-year-old Zonneveld could not capitalise, failing to take out 154 before Greaves finished with double eight to seal the victory.

Zonneveld will face defending champion Littler next and will need to beat him 5-2 or better in order to progress instead of the world number one.

Earlier in the day, Rob Cross started his campaign with a crushing 5-1 win to eliminate fifth seed Jonny Clayton, who suffered back-to-back defeats.

Clayton claimed the first leg but Cross surged back to win five in a row and finished with an average of 114.32, including three 180s.

Sixth seed Ross Smith was also knocked out despite edging a 5-4 thriller against German Gabriel Clemens.

The pair were neck and neck at 4-4 before Smith won the deciding leg, but his defeat by Rusty-Jake Rodriguez on Saturday meant that he could not qualify.

Northern Ireland's Josh Rock, who was eighth seed, is also out after defeat by Kevin Doets, while 15th seed Luke Woodhouse has been also eliminated.

Sports.title: LPGA Tour: Lindy Duncan wins The Annika for first title after 222 events
Sports.text:
The Annika final leaderboard

-16 L Duncan (US); -14 HJ Choi (Kor); -13 Y Yoshida (Jap), H Ryu (Kor); -12 J Lopez Ramirez (Spa); -11 G Lopez (Mex); -10 N Korda (US)

Selected others: -8 L Woad (Eng); -4 L Maguire (Ire), C Hull (Eng); +9 J Ewart Shadoff (Eng); +17 M Rhodes (Eng)

American Lindy Duncan was left "completely shocked" after winning her first LPGA Tour title at the 222nd time of asking.

The 35-year-old started Sunday's final round of The Annika with a one-shot lead and two late birdies saw her claim victory.

Duncan, who joined the tour in 2014, had only enjoyed one top-10 finish this season.

But her three-under-par 67 saw her finish on 16 under at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair, Florida, two shots clear of her nearest challenger, South Korea's Choi Hye-jin .

"I got so many people to thank that believed in me when I wasn't sure if I wanted to keep playing or if I was good enough to keep playing," Duncan said followng her win.

"To be here, I'm just completely shocked."

Duncan was tied for the lead with Choi with two holes left to play before her late heroics.

"Coming into today I kind of thought, 'No matter what happens I learned a huge lesson,' and hopefully I can take that forward with me," Duncan said.

"I just put so much pressure on myself because I really want to do well. Sometimes you just over try, and I think I've done that a lot. This week I finally let that go a little bit."

The win also saw her qualify as one of the 60 players at the season-ending CME Group Tour Championship by jumping from 74 to 34 in the standings for the season-long points race.

World number one Nelly Korda, who finished seventh, will be aiming to win her second season title next week.

England's Lottie Woad - another player in the field for next week's finale - was two shots further back but it was enough to secure a top-10 spot.

Gaming_Tech.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
Gaming_Tech.text:
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

But while Alice Huang is said to have stepped down from her role as Megaspeed director near the end of 2023, there were suspicions that she was still heavily involved in the firm's operations, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS

C4ADS said that Huang was still "practically in control" of Megaspeed even after she had handed over the reins of the firm.

Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.

Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before the Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the House Foreign Affairs and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.

The committee heads had threatened to issue subpoenas to Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.

Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued. Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.

"That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls," the congressman told the Face The Nation programme.

Separately, a group of tech leaders, including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.

A representative for Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times Sunday suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.

The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated to lead Nvidia is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.

The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next CEO from outside the company.

On Friday, Bessent had blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
