articles.title: Bessent blames Lutnick's department for Nvidia chip sales to Megaspeed
articles.text:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.

Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.

However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.

"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC, external.

"The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?

"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.

In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media.

Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.

Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang.

Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.

They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection.

A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.

"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

articles.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress about affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.

It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.

Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.

Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.

Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.

The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.

Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.

Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.

Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

articles.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.text:
A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.

The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.

Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.

"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.

He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.

"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.

The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.

The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".

Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.

The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.text:
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670m; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.

Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.

It has given Meta, which also runs WhatsApp and Instagram, 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.

The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech company.

A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.

The charge is related to a feature that suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. A preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery, according to the Italian regulator.

The regulator said it had taken into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact that the feature was "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".

It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation" in its decision.

Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law and the disproportionate level of the fine.

"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."

Last month, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
articles.text:
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.

Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.

Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table.

"At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"

Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".

He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".

The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer.

But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book".

"At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.

Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it".

"For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow.

"And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"

Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt.

"We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."

Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.

Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald.

"It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."

Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.

Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA.

"It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says.

"Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."

When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.

The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming.

"I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.

MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.

She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.

As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life".

"It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."

GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.

Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.

This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.

The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game.

"Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald.

"It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time.

"It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."

Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?

"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says.

"But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."

Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful".

"It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

articles.title: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
articles.text:
A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.

The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.

The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".

"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.

The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.

Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.

The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.

Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.

There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).

Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".

"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.

articles.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
articles.text:
At least 74 countries were affected by the Microsoft outage which was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.

Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, all experienced "connectivity problems", the company said.

As of early Friday afternoon (GMT), Microsoft was reporting improvements, with email queues "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption was widespread. Here is what happened around the world.

In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico, external their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."

Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems.

OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.

Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.

Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.

Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.

The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.

"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."

In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.

The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.

Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.

Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers might not be able to receive emails about their trips because of the outage.

Disruptions were also reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.

In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times, external.

The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.

"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.

Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".

Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.

In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".

In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.

Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.

Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.

European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.

Speaking to the same news agency, the head of Germany's BSI cybersecurity agency, Claudia Plattner, said the country's authorities had not been affected because they did not rely on Microsoft 365 services.

However, Reuters reported that Germany's national rail operator, Deutsche Bahn, was having difficulties sending out timetables for diverted trains due to the outage.

Plattner added the disruption was "affecting the whole world". "It is a global disruption that spans a vast number of data centres – stretching from Asia right across to the US, via Europe," she said.

In Antalya, Turkey, advisers and officials attending the UN Climate Change Conference, Cop31, were left frustrated by the outage.

James Young, a climate change adviser at the Inuit Circumpolar Council, the organisation which represents around 180,000 Inuit people living in the Arctic, told Reuters the council relied on emails and Microsoft Teams to communicate across several countries.

"It's just been really frustrating and challenging to maintain contact with our colleagues and to be able to effectively participate here," he said. "I think our dependence on technology leaves us vulnerable to situations like this."

In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies were among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.

Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.

"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa were unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.

However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

One winemaker in South Africa said almost his entire business had been brought to a "standstill" by the Microsoft outage.

"It's incredibly frustrating," Peter Pentz added. "We export a lot, so communication with exporters in Europe has come to a standstill."

Order processing, dispatch, communications and even "critical production work" were halted, he said, as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".

articles.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
articles.text:
Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.

Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.

NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.

Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.

The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.

The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.

Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.

The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.

NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.

Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.

There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.

The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.

Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.

In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".

Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.

That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.

Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.

Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.

Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal

MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place

The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage

MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework

Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.

Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.

But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.

Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.

Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed.

"We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.

Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.

articles.title: Holly Humberstone on her identity crisis - and struggle being compared to other pop stars
articles.text:
You might know her as a pop star, endorsed by everyone from Taylor Swift to Sam Fender, but Holly Humberstone has a secret double life.

In her spare time, the singer-songwriter is literally a cat burglar.

"We've stolen one of our neighbours' cats by accident," she laughs, in a Zoom call from her fixer-upper in New Cross, south-east London.

"He's a tiny little black cat who's come into our garden and simply chosen us."

Under the slightest scrutiny, however, her story crumbles like a biscuit in a hot cup of tea.

"OK, we've been coercing him into the house with treats," she admits. "He's just so cute.

"But we're not trying to keep him. We literally push him out every night."

Humberstone's excuse for this feline felony is that, last year, her parents sold her childhood home in Lincolnshire, external and moved to Wales – taking her pets with them.

One, a cat called Tsuki, had even been immortalised in the song Lucy as a confidante who listens to her problems but "never judges".

"Oh, she knows some secrets!" laughs the singer. "I'm so glad she can't talk."

"We actually tried to bring her to London with us, but she's a countryside cat and she hated it so much. We had to send her to Wales where she can be free and frolic."

Her parents' relocation was disruptive for the human Humberstones, too.

Their house, a "freezing cold, falling down" property 20 minutes outside of Grantham, played a huge part in the singer's success.

Her early EPs were all written there, inspiring the "wonky sonics" of her indie-leaning pop sound. The 2021 single Haunted House is even dedicated to the "friendly" spirits who inhabited the property.

"It's a place I always felt I could go back to, to remind myself of who I am," she says.

Instead, she spent 2025 "packing up 23 years of stuff my family and I had accumulated", from her old ballet shoes and poetry books to forgotten bits of jewellery.

The process was unsettling. Already grappling with the idea of leaving childhood behind, Humberstone found herself literally throwing away her past.

"I felt uprooted. I was having some sort of identity crisis almost weekly," she says.

So she did what she's always done, and poured those feelings into her second album, Cruel World, which entered the UK charts at number four earlier this year.

"Writing these songs felt like building myself a little shield and a kind of safety bubble," she says. "There's an escapist, fantasy element to so much of the album."

Maybe that's true, but Humberstone has always had the ability to locate a song's emotional core, and the lyrics on Cruel World don't disappoint.

"To lose somebody is to know you're only human, honey," she sings on To Love Somebody, external, soothing her elder sister as she endures an agonising break-up.

Undeterred by that heartbreak, she throws herself headfirst into a new affair on Die Happy, external, declaring: "Hit the gas, I want it fast, want it reckless."

But the most revealing song is the closing track, Beauty Pageant, external.

Fragile and raw, it's the sound of Humberstone in her dressing room, addressing the woman in the mirror who'd "die for the applause" but who struggles with the impossible beauty standards imposed on female artists.

"That's a song that I wasn't really setting out to write," she confesses.

"Writing about other people often feels easier than turning the magnifying glass on yourself."

The lyrics, she says, draw on a "very specific" mindset she acquired at her all-girls school in Grantham.

"It was drilled into me: You're all in competition. You're only rewarded if you're the best. And if you're not, you're worthless."

The experience "really warped the way I view other girls", she says.

Musical success made it worse. After winning the Brits Rising Star award in 2022, Humberstone found herself competing with megastars, even though her music leaned towards the alternative side of pop.

"I'm a very small fish and I recognise that, but suddenly I was in meetings being compared to all these people on my label's roster, who are on a completely different scale," she says.

"It's something I really, really struggled with in the early days and it's something I've really had to unlearn."

Nowadays, Humberstone has stopped benchmarking herself against her peers, recognising that the need for validation never fades.

"I don't think that there's a point I could get to, or an award that I could win, where these feelings would disappear," she says.

"Everybody feels like they've still got something to prove, so I'm done with setting myself goals - because then I lose sight of the real reason that I'm doing this, which is to write music that represents me, and have other people feel understood through that music."

Not that her mental health issues are in the rear view mirror. Humberstone admits her stage nerves have only intensified since the release of Cruel World.

"It's the proudest I've been of any of my work and, for that reason, I struggled with shows because I felt a lot of pressure to go out and deliver it to the standard that I think people are expecting.

"But on the other hand, it's totally fine if you mess up or sing a wrong note. People can't connect to a pop star that feels too robotic and polished.

"So maybe my strength is that vulnerability, and I need to recognise that more."

That vulnerability has won Humberstone millions of fans, even if a hit single has (so far) eluded her.

And her audience keeps growing. In May this year, her breakout single Falling Asleep At The Wheel was awarded a silver disc... five years after its release, indicating that her songs have staying power in an era of disposable hits.

Astonishingly, this is news to Humberstone, who learns about the accolade during our interview. But it helps to clarify a thought that's been knocking around her head.

"If I'm going to be doing this for years to come, I've just got to keep making music that feels right, trusting my gut and realising there's no end point," she says.

"Reaching an end point would mean I've 'made it', but I think, maybe, that's a myth that doesn't really exist."

articles.title: Hannah Fry feels 'unbelievably lucky' after cervical cancer treatment
articles.text:
Prof Hannah Fry has described feeling "unbelievably lucky" after being treated for cervical cancer.

The mathematician and BBC presenter, who recently took part in the second season of the Celebrity Traitors, said cancerous cells were discovered after she attended a cervical screening in 2020.

She underwent a hysterectomy, describing the experience to BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs as "horrific".

"As awful as that was, it had a full stop at the end of the sentence," the 42-year-old added. "I had my five-year clear the other day. I feel so unbelievably lucky."

In Sunday's episode, Fry told show host Lauren Laverne that she had delayed a cervical screening examination for months in 2020. After she attended one, the results "didn't come back for a few weeks," she said.

"Then I got a call from my GP telling me they needed me to come back and do another test, and they did a biopsy.

"I was trying hard not to panic but when they found it was in the lymphatic system… that was when it really started to come down."

The broadcaster said she was told that her chances of survival depended on the cancerous cells not having spread to her lymph nodes, although it was not clear "how bad it was at that point".

"It's all about, basically, how far into your lymphatic system has it got. If it had not got into any lymph nodes, then the odds were in my favour and I had a really good chance of survival," she said.

Fry explained that this meant "if it was in one it would drop to a 60% chance of survival and two – the odds would go against me and it would be a 40% chance".

While in isolation in hospital following her hysterectomy, Fry said a surgeon told her that four of her lymph nodes had appeared enlarged.

She added: "I was in this hospital bed on my own and no-one could come and visit me for over a week, with nothing but the sheer terrifying drop of the end of my existence in front of me – it was horrific."

Fry described not being able to "think back to happy things that... have already happened because it is sad", while also not being able to "look forward to things you are hopeful about because it doesn't feel like it is there".

She also said she asked her then husband to set up FaceTime in the corner of a room so she could watch their two young daughters play while she was in hospital.

"I didn't want them to see me, it was too much," she said.

But she added: "Going through something like that I don't think I would swap it.

"I think it was honestly such a gift to have that experience when you're 36 and then come out the other side of it."

The presenter grew up in a working-class family and studied mathematics at University College London.

She later completed a PhD in fluid dynamics, and last year became Cambridge University's first professor of the public understanding of mathematics.

Fry has fronted BBC science series including The Future with Hannah Fry and The Secret Genius of Modern Life.

She was banished in the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors after being exposed as a traitor.

articles.title: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.text:
A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.

Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.

None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny".

Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.

On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.

Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.

She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]."

She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.

Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

articles.title: Sotheby's auction of $180m Van Gogh challenged over claims it was 'sold under duress'
articles.text:
Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh.

Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), which carries an estimated value of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday.

But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Sotheby's says its own "extensive research" has not established this, but that it will work with the family to try and reach a solution.

"Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," the auction house told the BBC in a statement.

"We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history.

"While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognise the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution."

The painting is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says.

Four other owners have had it prior to it being put up for auction this year.

Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times, external, has written to Sotherby's on their behalf.

He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.

The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

articles.title: Eurovision Asia: Philippines wins continent's first song contest
articles.text:
The Philippines have won the very first Eurovision Song Contest Asia, hosted in Bangkok and with 11 countries vying for the title.

Nineteen-year-old singer Carmelle was always a front runner with her women's empowerment anthem Sobra-Sobra, complete with its catchy rap section.

She earned 211 points in total - 93 from the jury and 118 from the public vote - ahead of Thailand's MANG x DAOU in second place with 170 points.

There was a joyous atmosphere at the One Bangkok Arena as the crowd cheered the contestants and celebrated the popular winner.

Carmelle, the youngest contestant in the competition, was an obvious favourite with the juries and the public despite strong showings from several nations.

Other notable acts included MANG x DAOU, whose emotive duet Aroma elicited huge cheers from the home crowd.

Bangladeshi beatboxers Beatmosphere eschewed the traditional backing track, instead using their voices to replicate the sounds of drums and basslines.

And Laos's Thinla performed her crowd-pleasing song Bae in a traditional Lao hilltribe outfit.

However, the Laotian song had a unintentional second outing after the music video was played over an apparent technical issue during the broadcast - meaning it was the last song the audience heard before the vote.

The voting system worked much the same as the European Eurovison, with the public vote accounting for 50% of the result and the other 50% coming from the 11 national juries - with additional points awarded from a rest of the world vote.

Here's how the final scoreboard ended:

1. The Philippines - 211 points

2. Thailand - 170 points

3. Vietnam - 164 points

4. Malaysia - 152 points

5. Laos - 139 points

6. Bhutan - 126 points

7. Republic of Korea - 113 points

8. Mongolia - 94 points

9. Nepal - 69 points

10. Cambodia - 61 points

11. Bangladesh - 35 points

Also performing during the broadcast was 2026 Eurovision Song Contest winner Dara from Bulgaria, who performed her winning song Bangaranga and new song Bad Idea.

Thai superstar Jeff Satur also made an appearance, hitting the high notes in his performance of Black Tie.

Eurovision in Asia was an idea that has been talked about for decades, but one that never seemed to materialise - despite many false starts - until now.

There is a huge enthusiasm here for Eurovision Asia, but a large number of the audience were established fans of the original contest from other countries and regions of the world.

Speaking after the show, fan Zelie Pereira - who travelled from Scotland to Thailand to attend - said she was "very happy" with Carmelle's win.

articles.title: Noel Fielding 'appalled' by jokes he made with Russell Brand
articles.text:
Noel Fielding has said he is "appalled" by jokes he made alongside Russell Brand when the pair appeared together on TV and at live shows.

The Great British Bake Off presenter said in a statement to the Sun he was "horrified and deeply disturbed" to learn of Brand's crimes, after the disgraced comedian was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Footage of Fielding and Brand joking about rape with TV presenter Jonathan Ross on an episode of Channel 4's Big Fat Quiz of the Year in 2007 has resurfaced in the aftermath of Brand's conviction.

Fielding described "some of the jokes" he made as "horrible and inappropriate", and said he had not been in contact with Brand "for many years".

"I was horrified and deeply disturbed to learn of Russell Brand's crimes, which I was completely unaware of until they became public knowledge. My thoughts are with the women whose courage brought him to justice," Fielding said.

"I appeared on TV, radio and live charity shows with him, and whilst we played it up for the cameras and in the media, I considered it a professional relationship, rather than a personal one. I have had no contact with him for many years.

"Looking back at some of the jokes I made alongside him I was appalled. They were horrible and inappropriate, and I very much regret them."

Ross has also released a statement distancing himself from the remarks, saying that his "thoughts are with the many, many women who have bravely come forward."

Among the resurfaced footage is a clip of Brand and Fielding laughing on an episode of The Russell Brand Show, which aired on BBC Radio 2 in 2007. In it, Brand joked about kissing and holding an underage grasshopper.

"How do you even know if it's a child or an adult? You don't even care, do you," Fielding responded.

Brand can be heard replying: "It's a mistake I've made. I've had a lot of problems in the past, because I thought a grasshopper was above age. Before I know it, I'm in it, right, I'm kissing it, I'm holding it. Then it turns around and looks at me with onyx eyes and says: 'I'm 12.'"

Brand and Fielding also performed charity gigs together as The Goth Detectives.

articles.title: King Charles jokes with Elton John as he marks 78th birthday with radio show
articles.text:
King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

articles.title: Shane MacGowan: Tribute album gave mourning wife purpose
articles.text:
On the day of Shane MacGowan's funeral, his heartbroken wife found comfort in the same thing that moved and captivated the rest of the world that afternoon - the music that filled a parish church in Nenagh, County Tipperary.

Mundy and Camille O'Sullivan performed Haunted. Nick Cave sang A Rainy Night in Soho. And Glen Hansard and Lisa O'Neil led mourners in a send-off rendition of Fairytale of New York.

"I thought, well, if we just got all the people who were at the funeral on a record, that'd be something pretty special," Victoria Mary Clarke told BBC News NI.

On Friday, three years after her husband's death, that idea came to fruition with the release of 20th Century Paddy.

"It must be wonderful for Shane... I think up in heaven, he's very aware of what's going on," said Clarke.

There are 36 tracks on the new album - all penned by MacGowan - and 40 bands and soloists.

Among those are contributions from two acclaimed Irish artists who have passed away since recording their covers for the album.

Glen Hansard is featured performing Bottle of Smoke, while Moya Brennan provides her interpretation of Mother Mo Chroi.

"I feel love and connection between the artists (on the album) and Shane.

"And also, you know, for me personally, it feels like a lot of love because when somebody sends something nice to Shane, they're sending it to me."

The Pogues frontman died aged 65 at his Dublin home in 2023, following a hospital stay after being diagnosed with encephalitis.

Victoria was too fair to say who delivered her favourite cover on the album, but she was frank about how she personally benefited from the project.

"It gave me so much pleasure and it gave me so much joy and hope for the future to work on it because it gave me something to do every single day for three years and it got me out of bed and it got me to make new friends."

In the aftermath of her husband's death, that "social life and a sense of purpose" was invaluable to her.

But while the album is certainly bound up with MacGowan's death, it's not overshadowed by it.

"I think the artwork, if I had to pick, might be my favourite thing about the album," she chirped, an artist herself.

The term a 'who's who' doesn't quite capture the calibre and genre-defying diversity of the line-up featured on 20th Century Paddy.

There are hall-of-famers like Bruce Springsteen and Tom Waits.

Iconic, generation-crossing indie bands like The Jesus and Mary Chain and The Libertines.

And for anyone who needs reminding of how far above its weight Ireland punches when it comes to music, have a look at the back of 20th Century Paddy.

U2, Hozier and Bob Geldof - people with permanent residencies at top of the music industry.

There are stalwarts and custodians of the Irish folk tradition, Damien Dempsey perhaps foremost among them.

And lots of other artists, less established but very much in their ascendancy - Amble, Kingfishr and Madra Salach, to name but a few.

David Keenan, a singer-songwriter from Dundalk, whose thoughtful lyrics and intense live performances invoke something of MacGowan himself, told BBC News NI he was honoured to be asked to add to the album.

"Fairytale of New York is as old as Christmas for me," said David.

But his epiphany moment came when an uncle gave him The Pogues' third album.

At 11 years old, Keenan said If I Should Fall from Grace with God "lit a flame" inside him.

"Up 'til that point it was just chart music.

"That (album) was the first time I heard all these references to mythology and drink and rebellion and, you know, heartache.

"And poetry, proper poetry."

The Louth man described it like an awakening.

"It gave me permission as a kid to get stuck into real lyric writing. And to do it in the traditional and folk form."

On 20th Century Paddy, Keenan covered Sick Bed of Cúchulainn - a celtic punk ballad from their 1985 album Rum Sodomy and the Lash, the central allusion of which is the mythical Irish warrior Cúchulainn.

This has real significance for Keenan, who as a child in Louth used to play near the standing stone (Clochafarmore) where Cuchulainn was said to have been killed.

And the circularity didn't stop there.

He did his recording of the song in Drumlish, County Longford, where he said "Shane used to record too".

"It was just was surreal and at the same time perfect, you know."

Before putting his version down on tape, Keenan did something few artists would have done: he recited a poem he had written in Irish asking permission from MacGowan to sing the song.

"I felt connected to Shane's energy during the recording, you know."

Keenan said the quality of the artists on 20th Century Paddy showed the "global respect that was there for Shane's abilities, you know, as a lyric writer, a poet".

He added that, at a time when there is "a lot of pressure on young musicians now to go viral on TikTok and dumb themselves down... here's an artist who didn't do that".

"In an age of ChatGPT and generative AI", said Keenan, MacGowan is a reminder for "human beings to be authentic".

articles.title: Charlotte Church closes Powys wellness retreat after five years
articles.text:
Charlotte Church will close her wellness retreat after five "beautiful years", the company has announced.

The Dreaming, based in Rhydoldog House near Rhayader, Powys, offered retreats aimed at helping people reconnect with nature and spirituality.

The singer-songwriter bought the former home of fashion designer Laura Ashley in 2021, with its renovation later featuring in a Discovery Channel documentary series.

Last month, the team at the retreat announced it would be "pausing" operations to "reassess" what it should offer.

But it has now confirmed it is shutting down.

In a statement on social media, the team said they had hoped it would be a "period of hibernation, rather than an ending," but have come to realise it is the "end of our journey with The Dreaming".

"What a beautiful, wild and wonderful few years it has been," the post added.

According to documents filed to Companies House, external in March 2025, there were five employees at The Dreaming.

"We've shared stories, made friendships, held space for one another and found moments of stillness in a world that so rarely allows us to slow down.

"Thousands of you have found your way to this little corner of the Welsh hills, each bringing something of yourselves, and each leaving a little something behind. You have made The Dreaming what it is."

Last month the business said it was in the process of "germinating new dreams for the future" and was set to "hibernate".

Earlier this year, Church said that The Dreaming was a response to the pressures of contemporary life.

She said: "I am really passionate about what we do, because I believe more than ever the world and the people of the world are in dire need of being held through some very difficult times.

"There are some very difficult transitional times for us as human beings on this Earth.

"This is also due to the excesses in which society is so much based around, capitalist values and ideologies, meaning there is then less around care, people, community, nature and belonging. We are crying out for these things, every single one of us."

Church previously confessed she had blown "pretty much all my life savings" on the £1.5m, seven-bedroom property.

The house, with origins in the 15th Century, belonged to textile, fashion and retail entrepreneur Ashley and her husband Bernard and was owned by the family until his death in 2009.

A planning application for the retreat in 2021 said Church wanted to transform Rhydoldog House into a carbon neutral wellbeing and healing retreat with four log cabins in the grounds as tourist accommodation.

Since opening, The Dreaming hosted more than 3,000 guests and offered a "pay what you can" scheme starting at £1 per night, as well as free stays for NHS workers.

articles.title: Owain Wyn Evans completes Children in Need bike ride in Cardiff
articles.text:
Presenter Owain Wyn Evans has completed his challenge of cycling through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need.

The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show rode almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff on Friday.

The challenge started on 9 November in Scotland and over the next five days, Owain rode through Northern Ireland, England and Wales and raised £4,760,086 in the process.

Reflecting on his journey, he said: "This has been the hardest challenge of my life, 100%.

"I can't believe I'm here. It's overwhelming, all the love and passion and commitment people have shown."

In total, Children in Need raised £38.7 million in its 46th campaign.

The BBC said Owain's challenge would be the "greatest-ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity.

He crossed the finish line in Cardiff's Central Square just after 11:00 GMT, and was greeted by a crowd cheering him on before he was met by his husband, Arran Rees.

Owain, 42, whose bike was named Shania Chain, and decked out in Children in Need colours - Pudsey's favourite yellow with coloured spots - said: "Thank you so much everyone, from me and Shania.

"Honestly, this has felt so far away for such a long time. I can't believe that I'm here with this welcome and the sun's out."

Hollywood actor Luke Evans announced the route to Owain each day on BBC Radio 2.

During the 640km feat, he was also surprised with the premiere of Steps' brand-new version of their debut hit 5, 6, 7, 8, retitled 5, 6, 7, donate, which featured new lyrics and extra vocals.

It was recorded to help boost Owain's spirits on the longest day of his challenge.

The broadcaster also expressed his gratitude for the support of Radio 2 listeners.

His messages of support from public figures included one from the Princess of Wales, who recorded a message for him in Welsh, saying: "Hi Owain, it's Catherine, you're doing so well. Keep going. Wishing you all the very best."

Shania Twain was so impressed that the bike had been named after her that she sent a message of good luck before the challenge.

She said: "Hi Owain, Shania Twain here. You're about to take on an incredible challenge for BBC Children in Need, cycling 400 miles through all four nations.

"As you set off in Glasgow, I just want to say: 'Let's Go, Owain!' We'll be cheering you on all the way. Good luck."

She sent him another message when he finished, saying: "Congratulations on completing your incredible challenge for Children in Need. You're still the one my friend, sending you all my love."

Helen Thomas, head of Radio 2, said: "Owain truly captured the hearts of the nation this week as he battled through his epic four nations challenge.

"On behalf of all the Radio 2 listeners as well as the thousands of children and families who will benefit from his Herculean fundraising efforts we simply can't thank him enough. Diolch Owain! "

articles.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
articles.text:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.
